_comment: Quiz questions for the body-system modules. Original items written in-house. kind 'mcq': `answer` is the zero-based index of the correct option. kind 'identify': the learner selects a structure in the 3D workspace; `answer` lists accepted structure IDs, and selecting any part of an accepted structure also counts. Every item cites at least one reference and is a DRAFT until expert review.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a function of bones?
questions.explanation: Bones support, protect, store minerals and contain red marrow that makes blood cells. Pumping blood is the job of the heart.

questions.stem: Which bone is the longest in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone. The vertebral column is a chain of many bones, not one bone.

questions.stem: Which bones belong to the axial skeleton?
options: Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum
questions.explanation: The axial skeleton forms the central axis: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum. The girdles and limbs form the appendicular skeleton.

questions.stem: Which cells resorb (break down) bone matrix?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone; osteoblasts form it; osteocytes are mature bone cells in the matrix; chondrocytes are cartilage cells.

questions.stem: A displaced fracture of the femoral neck is most likely to threaten which of the following?
options: The blood supply to the femoral head
The sciatic nerve at the knee
The femoral artery in the adductor canal
questions.explanation: Vessels to the femoral head run along the femoral neck, so displaced neck fractures can interrupt them and cause avascular necrosis of the head.

questions.stem: Find the sternum (breastbone) on the 3D model.
questions.explanation: The sternum lies in the midline of the anterior chest wall; the ribs and clavicles attach to it.

questions.stem: Select a bone of the pelvic girdle.
questions.explanation: The pelvic girdle is formed by the two hip bones, which join the sacrum posteriorly at the sacro-iliac joints.

questions.stem: Which type of muscle is found only in the heart?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart wall. It is striated like skeletal muscle but works involuntarily.

questions.stem: Why do skeletal muscles usually work in pairs?
options: Because muscles can only pull, not push
Because each muscle needs a partner to receive blood
Because one muscle is always asleep
questions.explanation: A muscle can only shorten and pull. An opposing muscle (the antagonist) is needed to move the joint back.

questions.stem: Which ion, released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, triggers skeletal muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: Calcium binds troponin, moving tropomyosin off the binding sites on actin so myosin heads can attach and cycle.

questions.stem: The more mobile attachment of a muscle, which moves when it contracts, is called the:
questions.explanation: The insertion usually moves towards the origin, which is the more fixed attachment.

questions.stem: A patient has weakness with wasting, reduced tone and absent reflexes in one limb. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
options: Lower motor neuron (anterior horn cell or peripheral nerve)
questions.explanation: Wasting, low tone and absent reflexes are lower motor neuron signs. Upper motor neuron lesions give increased tone and brisk reflexes.

questions.stem: Find the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a dome of muscle and tendon separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities.

questions.stem: Select a pectoralis major muscle.
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major is the large fan-shaped muscle of the anterior chest wall; it adducts and medially rotates the arm.

questions.stem: Which blood vessels carry blood AWAY from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back. Capillaries connect the two.

questions.stem: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
options: Both sides equally, to each lung
Neither: blood reaches the lungs by gravity
questions.explanation: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the left atrium passes through which valve?
questions.explanation: The mitral (left atrioventricular) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle.

questions.stem: A person's stroke volume is 70 mL and heart rate 70 beats/min. What is the cardiac output?
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate = 70 mL × 70 /min = 4,900 mL/min, about 4.9 L/min.

questions.stem: A blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg is approximately equal to:
questions.explanation: 1 kPa ≈ 7.5 mmHg, so 120 mmHg ≈ 16.0 kPa and 80 mmHg ≈ 10.7 kPa.

questions.stem: Why does a fast heart rate reduce blood flow to the myocardium?
options: Coronary arteries fill mainly in diastole, which shortens most at high heart rates
The aortic valve closes the coronary ostia during diastole
The coronary veins are compressed in diastole
Heart rate has no effect on coronary flow
questions.explanation: Left coronary flow occurs mostly in diastole, when the myocardium relaxes. Diastole shortens more than systole as heart rate rises.

questions.stem: Find the heart on the 3D model.
questions.explanation: The heart lies in the middle mediastinum, behind the sternum and slightly to the left.

questions.stem: Select the vessel that returns blood from the lower body to the heart.
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava drains the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs into the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which two organs make up the central nervous system?
questions.explanation: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. Nerves outside them form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain mainly coordinates balance and smooth movement?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates movement, posture and balance.

questions.stem: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there?
questions.explanation: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

questions.stem: Which division of the autonomic nervous system dominates during 'rest and digest'?
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic division slows the heart and promotes digestion; the sympathetic division prepares for 'fight or flight'.

questions.stem: Why is lumbar puncture usually performed at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 level in adults?
options: The spinal cord usually ends at about L1–L2, so the needle enters below it
There is no cerebrospinal fluid above L3
The vertebrae are absent at these levels
questions.explanation: In adults the spinal cord usually ends at about L1–L2; below this the subarachnoid space contains nerve roots (cauda equina) and CSF, so the cord is avoided.

questions.stem: Find the cerebellum.
questions.explanation: The cerebellum lies at the back of the head, below the occipital lobes and behind the brainstem.

questions.stem: Select the part of the CNS that continues from the brainstem down the vertebral canal.
questions.explanation: The spinal cord continues from the medulla oblongata at the foramen magnum.

questions.stem: Where in the lungs does oxygen pass into the blood?
questions.explanation: Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries.

questions.stem: What happens to the diaphragm when you breathe in?
questions.explanation: The diaphragm contracts and flattens, enlarging the chest so air flows in.

questions.stem: How many lobes does the left lung normally have?
questions.explanation: The left lung has superior and inferior lobes; the right lung has three lobes.

questions.stem: Quiet expiration at rest is mainly produced by:
options: Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall
questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall recoil when the inspiratory muscles relax.

questions.stem: An inhaled peanut is most likely to lodge in which airway?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

questions.stem: Find the trachea (windpipe).
questions.explanation: The trachea runs from the larynx in the neck to its division into the main bronchi in the thorax.

questions.stem: Select the lung that has three lobes.
questions.explanation: The right lung has superior, middle and inferior lobes.

questions.stem: Where are most nutrients absorbed into the blood?
questions.explanation: The small intestine has a huge surface area (folds, villi, microvilli) and absorbs most nutrients.

questions.stem: What is the main job of the large intestine?
questions.explanation: The large intestine absorbs water and electrolytes and forms faeces.

questions.stem: Which organ produces bile?
questions.explanation: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the parts of the small intestine?
questions.explanation: Food passes from the stomach into the duodenum, then the jejunum, then the ileum.

questions.stem: Early appendicitis often causes pain around the umbilicus. Why?
options: The appendix is a midgut derivative, and midgut visceral pain is referred to the periumbilical region
The appendix lies behind the umbilicus
The umbilical vein drains the appendix
The pain comes from the abdominal wall muscles
questions.explanation: Visceral pain from midgut structures is referred to the periumbilical region; it moves to the right iliac fossa when the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.

questions.stem: Blood from the intestines reaches which organ before the general circulation?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut to the liver first, which explains first-pass metabolism of oral drugs.

questions.stem: Find the stomach.
questions.explanation: The stomach lies mainly in the upper left abdomen, below the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Select the organ that stores and concentrates bile.
questions.explanation: The gallbladder lies on the inferior (visceral) surface of the liver.

questions.stem: Which tube carries urine from each kidney to the bladder?
questions.explanation: Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the urinary bladder. The urethra carries urine out of the body.

questions.stem: Where in the nephron is blood first filtered?
questions.explanation: Filtration happens in the glomerulus into the glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.

questions.stem: Which hormone produced by the kidneys stimulates red blood cell production?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin from the kidneys stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells.

questions.stem: A normal glomerular filtration rate of about 125 mL/min equals roughly how much filtrate per day?
questions.explanation: 125 mL/min × 1,440 min/day ≈ 180,000 mL ≈ 180 L/day; almost all of it is reabsorbed.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a usual site where a ureteric stone lodges?
options: Where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim
questions.explanation: Stones lodge at the three narrowings of the ureter; the renal cortex is not part of the ureter.

questions.stem: Find a kidney.
questions.explanation: The kidneys lie on the posterior abdominal wall on either side of the vertebral column.

questions.stem: Select the organ that stores urine.
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder lies in the pelvis behind the pubic symphysis.

questions.stem: Which organs produce eggs (oocytes)?
questions.explanation: The ovaries produce oocytes and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.

questions.stem: Where does fertilisation usually take place?
questions.explanation: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube; the embryo then implants in the uterus.

questions.stem: Which cells of the testis produce testosterone?
questions.explanation: Leydig cells, between the seminiferous tubules, produce testosterone.

questions.stem: Why does benign prostatic hyperplasia cause difficulty passing urine?
options: The prostate surrounds the first part of the urethra and can compress it
The prostate weakens the bladder wall directly
questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra runs through the gland, so enlargement can obstruct urine flow.

questions.stem: Find the prostate.
questions.explanation: The prostate lies below the bladder, surrounding the first part of the male urethra.

questions.stem: How do hormones travel to their target cells?
questions.explanation: Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood, which carries them throughout the body.

questions.stem: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
questions.explanation: Insulin from the pancreatic islets lowers blood glucose; glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise it.

questions.stem: Which structure directly controls the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus releases hormones into the hypophysial portal vessels that control anterior pituitary secretion.

questions.stem: A fasting blood glucose of 5.0 mmol/L is approximately:
questions.explanation: 1 mmol/L ≈ 18 mg/dL, so 5.0 mmol/L ≈ 90 mg/dL, within the normal fasting range.

questions.stem: A pituitary tumour growing upwards classically causes which visual field defect?
questions.explanation: It compresses the optic chiasm, where nasal retinal fibres (serving the temporal fields) cross.

questions.stem: Find a suprarenal (adrenal) gland.
questions.explanation: The suprarenal glands sit on the superior poles of the kidneys.

questions.stem: Select the pituitary gland.
questions.explanation: The pituitary gland hangs below the hypothalamus in the hypophysial fossa of the sphenoid bone.

questions.stem: What is one main job of lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph; their lymphocytes respond to microbes and other antigens.

questions.stem: In which organ do T lymphocytes mature?
questions.explanation: T cells mature in the thymus ('T' for thymus); B cells mature in the bone marrow.

questions.stem: The thoracic duct empties into the venous system at the:
options: Junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins
Inferior vena cava at the kidneys
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle, where the left subclavian and internal jugular veins meet.

questions.stem: Why are people who have had their spleen removed advised to be vaccinated?
options: They are at greater risk of severe infection with encapsulated bacteria
They cannot produce red blood cells
They lose all their lymph nodes
Vaccines replace the spleen's filtering of bile
questions.explanation: The spleen is important in clearing encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus; vaccination reduces the risk.

questions.stem: Find the thymus.
questions.explanation: The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum, behind the sternum.

questions.stem: How does sweating help the body?
options: It cools the body as the sweat evaporates
questions.explanation: Evaporation of sweat removes heat from the skin surface.

questions.stem: Which vitamin does skin make when exposed to sunlight?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet B light converts a cholesterol derivative in the skin into vitamin D3.

questions.stem: Which skin layer contains blood vessels, nerves and hair follicles?
questions.explanation: The epidermis has no blood vessels; vessels, nerves and follicles lie in the dermis.

questions.stem: Why may a full-thickness burn be painless?
options: The nerve endings in the dermis are destroyed
Pain is always delayed by 24 hours
questions.explanation: A full-thickness burn destroys the dermis, including its sensory nerve endings.

questions.stem: Select the skin.
questions.explanation: The skin covers the whole external surface of the body.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye is light-sensitive?
questions.explanation: Photoreceptors (rods and cones) in the retina convert light into nerve signals.

questions.stem: Besides hearing, the inner ear is also responsible for:
questions.explanation: The vestibule and semicircular canals of the inner ear detect head position and movement.

questions.stem: Which structure provides most of the eye's refractive (focusing) power?
questions.explanation: The cornea provides most of the refractive power; the lens adjusts focus for near and far objects.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the auditory ossicles from the tympanic membrane inwards?
questions.explanation: The malleus attaches to the tympanic membrane, the incus links it to the stapes, and the stapes sits in the oval window.

questions.stem: Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected with which type of lens?
options: No lens: it cannot be corrected
questions.explanation: In myopia light focuses in front of the retina; a diverging lens moves the focus back onto the retina.

questions.stem: Find an eyeball.
questions.explanation: Each eyeball sits in its bony orbit, protected by the eyelids.

questions.stem: Select the lens of either eye.
questions.explanation: The lens lies behind the iris and is held by the suspensory ligament (zonular fibres).
